thread.title: Goldman Sachs and Apple are reportedly planning to cobrand a card (AAPL, GS)

author: Jaime Toplin
title: Goldman Sachs and Apple are reportedly planning to cobrand a card (AAPL, GS)
text:
facebook email copy link This story was delivered to Business Insider Intelligence " Payments Briefing " subscribers hours before appearing on Business Insider. To be the first to know, please click here .
Goldman Sachs and Apple will reportedly launch a new cobranded credit card early next year, according to The Wall Street Journal. The card, which will be part of a larger partnership between Apple and Goldman that extends to other services like financing, will likely be Apple Pay-branded and is expected to use the Visa network, though details remain scarce.
BI Intelligence
For Goldman, a credit card with a popular brand could be a smart move as the investment bank pushes into retail- and consumer-oriented services. Goldman has been bolstering GS Bank, its consumer business, in various ways: It first acquired GE Capital, then launched lending arm Marcus in 2016, and most recently acquired Final, which signaled an interest in credit cards.
The Apple deal extends that push, and could represent Goldman's ticket to consumer credit success. Marketing with Apple could be an easy way to spread recognition of its offerings and pick up new customers, especially if the program offers a strong rewards proposition — the top reason customers choose credit cards. In addition, the deal should replace Apple's existing Barclays-issued cobrand, according to The Wall Street Journal, which could give Goldman access to an existing customer base.
If the card, which marks the first major diversification of the Apple Pay brand beyond mobile, is a hit, it could help galvanize the wallet's lagging adoption. The move could increase brand recognition for Apple Pay. Mobile wallet adoption in the US is currently lagging, hovering around a quarter of eligible users. And growth has been relatively stagnant in adoption. By branding a credit card with Apple Pay, Apple is bringing its mobile payments brand to hard plastic — the most popular US payment method — which could ultimately grow awareness of the wallet.
That could improve adoption, which ultimately benefits Apple. Though the card itself isn't directly tied to mobile payments, it could help consumers form daily habits around the Apple Pay brand, which might make them more willing to put the card into their wallet and try it.
The card could also be more appealing to existing Apple Pay super users who want to engage more with the brand, especially if the firms opt to reward users for mobile payments specifically — something other banks have done, and which Apple could have an incentive to do, since the cobrand might allow it to increase the share of interchange it collects for each digital transaction. That, in turn, could boost adoption and engagement, which might bring gains to Apple's services revenue segment.
